sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Boletus edulis is a stout bolete with a smooth bun-shaped brown cap, often paler at the margin. The underside has tiny pores, never gills: they are white when young, then yellow to olive with age. Its pale, thick stem usually carries a fine raised whitish net, especially near the top. There is no ring or volva.

sections.title: Cut surface and spores
sections.text: The firm flesh remains white when cut or bruised; the pores and tubes do not turn blue. The spore print is olive brown. Individual spores are elongated under a microscope.

sections.title: Ecology and season
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal fungus fruits on soil near trees, including beech, birch, oak, pine and spruce. In Europe it is found mainly from summer into autumn, depending on weather and site.

sections.title: Comparison and food safety
sections.text: Tylopilus felleus may have pinkish pores and a darker stem net and is intensely bitter. Red or orange pores, obvious blue staining, or gills point away from B. edulis. A single feature or drawing cannot establish edibility. Eat only specimens identified with certainty, fresh and properly cooked; some people still develop digestive symptoms.

traits: Brown bun-shaped cap with a paler margin
White pores when young, turning yellow then olive; no gills
Pale stout stem with whitish reticulation, most visible near the top
White flesh and pores do not stain blue
safetyNote: Edible only after reliable identification. Examine the pore surface, whole stem and cut flesh; a picture alone cannot confirm a wild mushroom. Use fresh specimens and cook thoroughly. Seek poison-centre advice if illness follows consumption.
